purpose: Fluvoxamine is mainly used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), which involves unwanted, repeated thoughts or behaviors that are hard to control. It can also help with social anxiety disorder and sometimes depression. It helps reduce anxiety and the urge to perform compulsive rituals.
how_it_works: Your brain uses a chemical called serotonin to help regulate mood and anxiety. Fluvoxamine works by keeping more serotonin available in the spaces between brain cells, so it can do its job better. Think of it like keeping a helpful messenger active longer so your brain can communicate more effectively and feel calmer.
common_side_effects: Nausea (especially when you first start), sleepiness or trouble sleeping, headache, dry mouth, dizziness, sweating, decreased appetite, and upset stomach. Most of these tend to improve after the first couple of weeks as your body adjusts.
warnings: Do NOT take fluvoxamine with certain medications — especially MAOIs like phenelzine or selegiline — as this combination can be dangerous. It may increase suicidal thoughts in children, teens, and young adults, especially early in treatment, so watch for mood changes and contact your doctor right away if this happens. Tell your doctor about all medicines you take, since fluvoxamine interacts with many drugs. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
typical_dosing: Adults usually start with 50 mg taken once a day at bedtime. The dose may be slowly increased by your doctor every week or two as needed, up to a maximum of 300 mg per day. If your daily dose goes above 100 mg, it is usually split into two doses — one in the morning and one at night. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
